draft.title: Technique, example and effect
card: Technique
Name the technique the writer uses, such as metaphor, repetition or a short sentence.
Example
Give the words or moment that show it. Keep any quotation short and say exactly where the technique is.
Effect
Explain what the technique makes the reader think or feel. Use verbs such as suggests, creates or emphasises.
Then link the effect to your argument. Say how it helps prove your thesis. Most marks are earned here, not in naming the technique.
draft.remember: Naming a technique is only the start. Explain what it does and how it proves your point.

a.q: Which sentence from an analytical paragraph includes a technique, an example and an effect?
opts: The simile "like a locked door" suggests the town fears outsiders
The writer uses a simile to describe the town in the story
The town is described as "like a locked door" by the writer
The writer uses a simile, a metaphor and a list for the town
a.why: The first option names the simile, gives the example and explains what it suggests. The second names a technique but gives no example or effect. The third gives an example but only describes it, so it explains nothing.
a.clue: Look for the sentence that says what the words make the reader think.

b.q: A student writes: "The repeated word 'alone' appears three times in the poem." The student's argument is that the speaker feels isolated. What is the main thing missing from this sentence?
opts: An explanation of what the repetition does for the argument
The name of the technique, which is repetition
A longer quotation from the poem to prove the point
A second technique from the same part of the poem
b.why: The student has named the technique and given the example, so the sentence only describes. It needs to explain what the repetition makes the reader feel and link that to isolation. A longer quotation is tempting, but more evidence does not replace explanation.
b.clue: The sentence says what is there, but not what it does.
